summary: A perspective on the ARPANET Reference Model, pointing out differences from the ISO Reference Model raised by working group members over the years. It was originally published by MITRE.

eli5.summary: Two teams had different ideas about how to organize network layers. This paper compares them.

how does arm differ from osi model

subtitle: Explaining the architectural principles behind ARPANET and TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET pioneered practical intercomputer networking, but its designers never formally documented the underlying reference model, leaving newcomers to the field to misunderstand its principles compared to the ISO model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 871 articulates the ARPANET Reference Model (ARM) through seven core axioms: resource sharing, interprocess communication, logical connections, layering, virtualization, efficiency, and equity. It explains how these axioms shaped TCP/IP and differ fundamentally from the ISO Reference Model (ISORM).
tldr.outcome: The document provides historical context for why ARPANET protocols are designed as they are and why the ARM's pragmatic approach differs from—and arguably predates—the more formal ISO model.

today: RFC 871 is a foundational historical document. The ARPANET itself is Historic, but the ARM as articulated here remains relevant to the design of the modern Internet. TCP/IP, built on these principles, became the global standard. While the ISORM influenced some protocol designs and standards bodies, the ARM's pragmatic approach—emphasizing resource sharing, architectural flexibility, and equitable implementation—continues to guide Internet protocol development today.

sections.title: The Case for Explaining ARPANET's Model
sections.content:
By the 1980s, the ARPANET had proven that intercomputer networking was possible and practical, yet most attention had shifted to the ISO's Reference Model for Open System Interconnection (ISORM). This created a misconception: that the ARPANET had no deliberate design philosophy.

In fact, the ARPANET Network Working Group (NWG) consisted of system programmers and computer scientists from DARPA-sponsored research institutions who developed a coherent reference model as they designed TCP/IP and the original ARPANET protocols. That model was largely tacit: it guided decisions rather than appearing in formal documentation.

This RFC, written by M. A. Padlipsky (one of the designers), articulates the ARM publicly for the first time. The goal is not to criticize the ISORM but to explain the ARM's roots and show that it remains a viable alternative, particularly given that the ARPANET's basic ideas preceded the ISO work.
sections.eli5: ARPANET worked great, but nobody ever wrote down why. Now someone who was there explains: Here are the big ideas we actually used, and here's why they're good.

sections.title: The Seven Axioms of the ARM
sections.content:
Resource Sharing is the fundamental goal: intercomputer networking enables heterogeneous operating systems (Hosts) to share programs and data cooperatively, beyond mere remote access. This axiom makes protocols like X.25, which only offer remote login, less interesting to the ARM perspective.

Interprocess Communication is the mechanism: resource sharing happens via communication between active processes (programs in execution), not between procedures or systems. This axiom assumes familiarity with operating systems but does not assume tight coupling between Hosts.

Logical Connections address demultiplexing: processes distinguish between multiple communication channels through socket numbers and Well-Known Sockets (W-KS), where services reside at known ports. This adds semantics to addressing.

Layering organizes protocols into functional groupings where lower-layer protocols treat upper-layer control information as opaque data. The ARM uses three broad layers (Network Interface, Host-Host, Process-Level) with modular protocols within them, contrasting with the ISORM's seven narrower layers where N-entities must communicate via N-1 entities.

Common Intermediate Representations (virtualizing) solve what Padlipsky calls the 'N x M Problem': if N different operating systems each must support M different terminal or file types, the result is unmanageable complexity. The virtual terminal and virtual file concepts map native representations to a common format, enabling flexibility.

Efficiency is a stated concern: protocols should follow the principle of Parsimony (least mechanism). The ARM allows protocols within a layer to interact directly where appropriate, avoiding the overhead of traversing a strict protocol hierarchy when not necessary.

Equity requires that protocol mechanisms integrate equitably with participating operating systems. The ARMS designers listened to implementation feedback and adjusted mechanisms that would unfairly burden particular systems.
sections.eli5: The ARM has seven big ideas: 1) Share resources, not just access. 2) Use interprocess communication. 3) Use port numbers for addressing. 4) Layer protocols. 5) Use common formats. 6) Be efficient. 7) Be fair to all operating systems.

sections.title: The Three-Layer Architecture
sections.content:
The Network Interface Layer contains protocols between Hosts and the communications subnetwork (CSNP; for example, packet switches). The key property is that bits sent to this layer will probably reach their destination, but delivery is not guaranteed. Different types of CSNPs may be interconnected via Gateways (special-purpose systems that attach to multiple networks). A Network Interface protocol is typically invoked by the Host-Host layer but may be invoked by Process-Level protocols or even by raw host processes.

The Host-Host Layer provides interprocess communication functionality, enabling processes to communicate with processes on other Hosts, even across multiple networks. This layer may offer reliability, flow control, and handling of out-of-band signals, though these are not mandatory. The current Internet version adds the ability to route across proximate networks using Gateways. A Host need not be sophisticated; even an intelligent terminal may de facto constitute a single process.

The Process-Level/Applications Layer contains protocols for resource sharing and remote access: login, file transfer, mail, and similar services. These protocols often use Common Intermediate Representations but are not required to. Protocols at this layer may invoke other protocols in the same layer or lower layers as appropriate for their operating system context.

Orthogonally, a Host may implement protocols inboard or delegate them to an Outboard Processing Environment (for example, a Network Front End) via a Host-Front End protocol, provided the Host appears functionally identical from the perspective of other Hosts.
sections.eli5: Imagine three floors in a building: the basement handles talking to the phone lines (Network Interface). The ground floor routes messages between neighbors (Host-Host). The upper floors are the actual services such as email, file sharing, and chat (Process-Level).

sections.title: TCP and IP Design Goals
sections.content:
TCP/IP emerged from three recognizable goals. First, internetting enables Hosts on different networks to communicate. Second, reliability fixes limitations of the original ARPANET Host-Host Protocol (AH-HP), which relied on the communications subnet for error recovery. If internetting involved less reliable subnets, TCP had to provide end-to-end reliability. Third, a good Host-Host protocol retains useful ideas from AH-HP (sockets, logical connections, Well-Known Sockets, interprocess communication) while replacing flawed mechanisms.

Three design constraints follow: Layering means TCP and IP must operate in a layered hierarchy, which also justifies separating internetting (IP) from Host-Host reliability (TCP). Minimal subnet assumptions means the protocols make no demands on the properties of communications subnetworks they traverse, allowing TCP to virtualize the underlying subnet for its users. Minimal Host assumptions means Hosts need not be powerful; they must understand processes and be able to keep time (or simulate timing), but even a modest machine can participate.
sections.eli5: TCP/IP was designed for three reasons: connect different networks, make communication reliable, and create good protocols. It uses three rules: keep layers clean, assume subnets are not special, and do not demand much from the computers using it.

sections.title: Gateways and Internetworking
sections.content:
A Gateway is a special system that attaches to two or more communication subnetworks as if it were a Host. From the network's point of view, Gateways are indistinguishable from Hosts. However, Gateways interpret a full version of IP that handles routing between networks and fragmentation of datagrams to fit different subnetwork sizes. Host IP implementations may use a simpler, static view of routing.

Crucially, Gateways do not translate or map between dissimilar protocols above IP (for example, TCP to AH-HP, or ARPANET FTP to other FTP variants). This is an explicit assumption of the ARM: the catenet (concatenated internet) is 'protocol compatible' at higher levels. The justification is complex but broadly sound: protocol translation is lossy and hard to maintain, and interoperability is better achieved through agreement on common protocols.
sections.eli5: Gateways connect different networks but do not translate between different protocols. They are like border guards who check routing but do not translate languages—everyone has to speak the same protocol above the network layer.

sections.title: ARM vs. ISORM
sections.content:
The ARM and ISORM share some principles, both value layering, connections, and higher-level protocol sophistication, but differ fundamentally in philosophy. The ISORM prescribes a strict seven-layer hierarchy where N-entities must communicate via N-1 entities, even within a single Host. This avoids some design questions but enforces artificial boundaries and overhead.

The ARM treats layers as broad functional groupings (Network, Host-Host, Process-Level) whose modularity comes from clean interfaces and expertise in protocol design, not from multiplying layers. Within a layer, protocols can interact directly where it makes sense. At the Host-Host layer, for example, TCP and UDP share IP, and either can be used by applications without artificial separation.

The ARM also emphasizes resource sharing rather than mere remote access; virtualizing (Common Intermediate Representations) as a practical tool rather than a universal mandate; and efficiency through Parsimony rather than strict prescriptive rules. The Principle of Equity—ensuring protocols integrate equitably with different operating systems—is explicit in the ARM but largely absent from the ISORM.

Padlipsky argues that the ARM's descriptive (rather than prescriptive) approach allows it to remain flexible and practical as networks evolve, whereas the ISORM's attempt to prescribe everything creates rigidity and complexity.
sections.eli5: ISORM says: 'Every message must climb down seven floors and back up seven floors, always.' ARM says: 'Use as many layers as you need, and talk directly when it makes sense.' ARM is more flexible; ISORM is more rigid but tries to be more precise.

left.title: ARM Approach
left.desc: Broad layers, modular protocols within layers, direct interaction when sensible, flexibility and efficiency prioritized.

right.title: ISORM Approach
right.desc: Narrow layers, strict N+1 hierarchy, all N-entities talk via N-1, precision and completeness prioritized.
